rationale: B wins because its best angles are built around reportable accountability questions, not product gloss: "Who eats the fine when the AI misclassifies a contractor?" gives an employment-law reporter a real sourcing path. A has smart material, but "Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire. AI Is Moving It to the Moment of the Decision" turns one product detail into a category claim the update does not prove. B still overreaches in places, but its refusals and proof asks would keep the founder out of more trouble.
gaps_in_A: "raises a pointed question about the competitive pressure driving the launch" builds a bridge between the lawsuit and product launch that the update does not establish.
"Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire" is an unsupported before/after claim; the facts only say Deel's tool checks risk as a company hires.
"Deel's launch is the first concrete product" invents market position. One launch is not proof of firstness or category shift.
"No Extra Cost. That's a Bet on Moat Over Margin" overreads "included for existing customers" into a pricing and margin strategy without confirmation.
gaps_in_B: "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" is not in the facts. Deel handles compliance; the update does not say it previously sold this layer separately.
"competitor pricing responses land within weeks" invents a future reaction. That is a forecast, not grounding.
"Who eats the fine" is a strong hook, but fines and statutory penalties need outside sourcing; the update says tax exposure and classification risk, not penalty mechanics.
"Find a real current signal before pitching" is too restrictive for trade and accountability press. The launch is already a valid why-now; a stronger external peg would help, but it is not mandatory.
